description.text: Our mission is to transform the health of the communities we serve, one person at a time. As the nation's largest managed care company focused on underserved populations, Centene is committed to helping people live healthier lives. Centene offers affordable and high-quality products to more than 1 in 15 individuals across the nation, including Medicaid and Medicare members (including Medicare Prescription Drug Plans) as well as individuals and families served by the Health Insurance Marketplace. Centene provides access to high-quality healthcare, innovative programs and a wide range of health solutions that help families and individuals get well, stay well and be well. We believe the best way to deliver healthcare is with a personal approach, with local brands and local teams who live in, care about and directly influence the communities they serve – a key differentiator in our ability to provide access to quality care for our members. Our state-based plans are built on community expertise and backed by the depth, breadth, and experience of a leading national company. Our model is structured around partnership. By working hand-in-hand with providers, policymakers, and communities, we connect people to what matters most – not just healthcare, but essentials like food, housing, utilities, and transportation – to drive meaningful health outcomes. With our scale and expertise, we are not only improving lives but also shaping the future of healthcare.

about.description_short: Centene Corporation, a Fortune 500 company, is a leading healthcare enterprise that is committed to helping people live healthier lives. The Company takes a local approach - with local brands and local teams - to provide fully integrated, high-quality and cost-effective services to government-sponsored and commercial healthcare programs, focusing on under-insured and uninsured individuals. Centene offers affordable and high-quality products to nearly 1 in 15 individuals across the nation, including Medicaid and Medicare members (including Medicare Prescription Drug Plans) as well as individuals and families served by the Health Insurance Marketplace and the TRICARE program. The Company also contracts with other healthcare and commercial organizations to provide a variety of specialty services focused on treating the whole person.

analysis_md:
# CNC — Centene Corporation
v5 run, 2026-10-14. Price $69.29 (nasdaq_quote_api, key_numbers.md). Engine market-cap estimate $34.169B — in scope under $40B.

All figures below are copied from key_numbers.md, dcf_numbers.json, financials_history.csv, or ttm.py output — none are recomputed. Earnings-release and research facts are from cited web searches (see Research notes inline).

## What it is
The largest US Medicaid managed-care organization: government-sponsored health insurance across three books — Medicaid (the core, ~29-state footprint), ACA Marketplace plans under the Ambetter brand, and Medicare (Medicare Advantage plus a fast-growing standalone prescription-drug-plan business, 8.8M PDP members in Q2 2026). Q2 2026 (reported Jul 28, 2026): total revenue $53.6B (+~10% YoY), premium and service revenue $44.4B (+4% YoY), adjusted diluted EPS $2.51 vs a $(0.16) loss a year earlier, consolidated health benefits ratio (HBR) 89.6% vs 93.0% a year earlier. Membership is shrinking even as margins repair: Medicaid 12.1M members (−5.5% YoY, full-year 2026 guided down 8–9%), Marketplace 3.5M vs roughly 5.9M a year earlier after enhanced-subsidy expiry.

## Owner's earnings
**FY2025 (10-K via EDGAR, from financials_history.csv):** operating cash flow $5,088,000,000; capex $767,000,000 (tag PaymentsToAcquirePropertyPlantAndEquipment); SBC $204,000,000 (tag ShareBasedCompensation — always a real cost); net income −$6,674,000,000.
- **Conservative owner's earnings FY2025: $4,117,000,000 = $8.35/share** (key_numbers.md: latest FY OE/share $8.35, latest FY OE total $4.117B).
- Maintenance version FY2025 (NI + D&A − min(capex, D&A) − ΔNWC, from financials_history.csv): −$2,217,000,000 — the two definitions are $6B+ apart in the same year, which is itself the central warning on this name: for a managed-care insurer the OCF-based figure rides premium/claims working-capital and reserve timing, not distributable earnings.
- OE positive 4 of the last 5 fiscal years (key_numbers.md) — the negative year is FY2024 (conservative OE −$702,000,000, from financials_history.csv), when OCF collapsed to $154,000,000 despite positive net income.
- Balance sheet (folded in explicitly): net debt −$487.0M, i.e. net cash (key_numbers.md); net debt / normalized OE −0.12x (diagnostics). Holding-company leverage is not the risk here; reserve adequacy and government rate-setting are. Research cross-check: debt-to-capitalization improved to 41.6% at Q2 2026 from 46.5% at year-end 2025 (Q2 2026 earnings coverage).

**Base used = the engine's normalized base: $8.35/share, median of the last 3 FY OE/share** (base_source: median_of_last_3_fy_oe_per_share; latest FY and normalized are both $8.35 — the median year and the latest year coincide). No TTM pin was used — see the STALE_FY resolution below for the full TTM quote and the written reason the TTM base was rejected for this insurer.

## Moat: 4/10 — weak
Justification: the largest US Medicaid managed-care organization with incumbency across a ~29-state footprint, the leading ACA Marketplace franchise (Ambetter), and growing Medicare PDP scale (8.8M members in Q2 2026) at a lean 7.4% adjusted SG&A ratio — real scale advantages in government-program procurement. Against that: the customer is the government, rates are set politically and contracts are rebid, so there is no pricing power; Medicaid federal funding cuts and redeterminations are shrinking the rolls (FY2026 Medicaid membership guided down 8–9%); ACA enhanced-subsidy expiry already cut Marketplace membership from ~5.9M to 3.5M YoY; and insurer margins are razor-thin (FY2025 HBR 91.9%), leaving earnings hostage to medical-cost inflation in behavioral health, home health and high-cost drugs. Morningstar assigns managed-care names at most a narrow moat and Centene none — consistent with a weak 4/10.
- FOR: #1 US Medicaid MCO — largest Medicaid footprint, incumbency across ~29 states in contract rebids
- FOR: Ambetter — leading ACA Marketplace franchise
- FOR: Medicare PDP scale — 8.8M members in Q2 2026 and growing
- FOR: Lean cost structure — FY2025 adjusted SG&A expense ratio 7.4%
- AGAINST: Government is the customer — rates set politically, no pricing power, contracts rebid
- AGAINST: Medicaid policy headwinds — federal funding cuts and redeterminations; FY2026 Medicaid membership guided -8% to -9%
- AGAINST: ACA subsidy expiry — Marketplace membership fell from ~5.9M to 3.5M YoY in Q2 2026
- AGAINST: Razor-thin insurer margins — FY2025 HBR 91.9% leaves no buffer against medical-cost spikes
- AGAINST: Medical-cost inflation exposure — behavioral health, home health, high-cost drugs, No Surprises Act disputes
- A 4 gives CAP = 7.2 years: growth holds 2 years, then converges linearly to the 2.5% terminal rate over 7.2 years, 15-year projection.

## DCF — v5 final run (--moat 4, probs 0.15/0.30/0.30/0.20/0.05, offsets recalibrated, default mults)
**Growth sanity check (mandatory):** the engine's g_base is 14.89% (blend 9.89% plus the +5.00% share-count adjustment). Its components overstate a forward growth rate for this name: latest revenue YoY is 19.98%, but the current print is far lower — Q2 2026 premium and service revenue grew only +4% YoY (the +~10% total-revenue print is mostly premium-tax pass-through), membership is shrinking in both Medicaid (guided −8% to −9% for FY2026) and Marketplace, and the OE/share CAGR 2y component is −19.53%. Scenario starts were therefore recalibrated downward via offsets (−0.199 / −0.129 / −0.079 / −0.029 / +0.031 vs g_base) to −5% / +2% / **+7%** / +12% / +18%: base +7% ≈ premium-yield growth plus early HBR margin repair plus a fading buyback tailwind; bull/super-bull are margin-repair cases (HBR normalizing from the FY2025 91.9% level, as Q2 2026's 89.6% print began to show), not membership-growth cases. Probabilities were skewed defensive (15/30/30/20/5 vs the 10/25/30/25/10 default) for the federal Medicaid policy overhang, partly offset by the Q2 2026 beat and the raised FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance (to greater than $4.80, from greater than $3.00 — with roughly $0.50 of the raise attributed by management to non-recurring items, per Q2 coverage). Price $69.29.

| Scenario | Prob | Growth start | OE mult | Story | IV@15 | IRR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Super bear | 15% | -5.0% | 0.75 | Medical-cost spiral repeats; Medicaid rates lag acuity again; membership shrink compounds | $38.35 | 9.17% |
| Bear | 30% | 2.0% | 0.90 | HBR repair stalls in the low-90s; rate increases only match cost trend | $60.41 | 13.39% |
| Base | 30% | 7.0% | 1.00 | Premium yield + early margin repair + fading buyback tailwind | $81.28 | 17.08% |
| Bull | 20% | 12.0% | 1.10 | HBR normalizes toward the high-80s and holds; PDP scale compounds | $107.95 | 21.32% |
| Super bull | 5% | 18.0% | 1.25 | Full margin repair plus rate catch-up across Medicaid and Marketplace | $153.21 | 27.59% |

- **Probability-weighted: IV@15% $77.51 (+11.9% vs price), IV@12% $102.99 (+48.6%), IV@10% $131.40, weighted IRR 16.42%, base-case IRR 17.08%**
- **Tier by numbers: B.** Diagnostics (key_numbers.md): OE yield 12.05%, terminal value 18.7% of IV@15%, scenario spread 4.00x, net debt −0.12x normalized OE, 9.4 months since FY end.

## Flags — every fragility flag resolved
- **STALE_FY** (latest fiscal year ended 9.4 months ago): ttm.py was run and succeeded; its full inputs are quoted here, and the TTM base was then **rejected as the pin, with the reason stated**: OCF FY $5,088,000,000 − prior YTD $3,295,000,000 + current YTD $7,956,000,000 = TTM $9,749,000,000; capex FY $767,000,000 − prior YTD $343,000,000 + current YTD $374,000,000 = TTM $798,000,000; SBC FY $204,000,000 − prior YTD $94,000,000 + current YTD $126,000,000 = TTM $236,000,000; shares (current-YTD weighted diluted) 496,605,000; TTM OE total $8,715,000,000 → TTM OE/share $17.55 (ttm.py output: 17.549158788171685). That TTM figure is more than double the $8.35 median base, and the gap is managed-care cash timing, not earnings power: the TTM window ends June 30 and captures an H1-weighted premium/claims and settlement cycle (current YTD OCF alone is $7,956,000,000), while FY2024 proved a full year of this company's OCF can print $154,000,000. Cross-checks agree the TTM OE is not a distributable-earnings base: FY2025 adjusted EPS was $2.08 and FY2026 adjusted EPS is guided to greater than $4.80 (earnings releases via search) — both far below even the median OE base. The engine's median base is therefore used, per the BASE_DIVERGENCE logic of deciding which base is distorted: here the TTM is the distorted one. If a future run's TTM window shows the H1 OCF surge annualizing into a full-year print, this decision should be revisited.
- **BUYBACK_TAILWIND** (share count shrinking 5.4%/yr): real historically — share count CAGR −5.38% with the +5.00% growth adjustment already credited in g_base (key_numbers.md), and not double-counted in the verdict. Current evidence says it is fading: ttm.py's share legs show current-YTD weighted diluted shares of 496,605,000 vs the FY2025 figure of 493,116,000 — the buyback did not shrink the count in H1 2026 — which is one reason scenario growth starts were recalibrated downward rather than letting the full historical tailwind compound.
- **NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE** (net income and operating cash flow differ by >40% in 2023, 2024, 2025): structural insurer working capital plus named one-offs, different each year — from financials_history.csv: 2023 net income $2,702,000,000 vs OCF $8,053,000,000 (favorable claims/reserve and premium timing); 2024 net income $3,305,000,000 vs OCF $154,000,000 (the timing reversed — a profitable year on paper produced almost no operating cash); 2025 net income −$6,674,000,000 vs OCF $5,088,000,000 (the GAAP loss was driven largely by non-cash goodwill and divestiture-related impairment charges taken in 2025, per FY2025 earnings coverage, while cash generation recovered and HBR hit 91.9%). Because the sign of the divergence flips year to year, neither net income nor a single year's OCF is a trustworthy base on its own — the 3-year median OE base is the least-distorted of the engine's options, and the residual model risk is handled via low confidence and the tier softening in the verdict.
- **WIDE_SCENARIO_SPREAD** (flagged on the preliminary run; final-run diagnostics show a 4.00x spread, key_numbers.md): real — a government-rate-dependent insurer's 15-year range genuinely runs from a renewed medical-cost spiral (super-bear IV@15% $38.35, well below the $69.29 price) to full margin repair ($153.21). Consequence: confidence is low and the verdict is sized to the conservative end.

## My thoughts / overlay
- **Method range is the headline.** On the engine's OCF-based numbers this is a Tier B (weighted IRR 16.42%, only ~1.4pp above the 15% hurdle, on a base that is itself an upper bound for an insurer). On any earnings-based reading — FY2025 adjusted EPS $2.08, FY2026 guided above $4.80 against an $8.35 OE base — the same cash flows clear 15% only at a materially lower price, in words; the TTM OE of $17.55/share would print the opposite extreme. The defensible range therefore spans C to B, and the verdict takes the conservative end. As with HIG, this is the insurer artifact: premiums collected are not owner cash until claims and reserves settle.
- Quality/recovery evidence is genuinely improving: Q2 2026 HBR 89.6% vs 93.0% a year earlier, commercial HBR 79.2% in Q2 2026 vs 95.4% in Q4 2025, Medicaid HBR stabilizing (93.0% in Q4 2025, a 40bp sequential improvement per the FY2025 release), guidance raised twice during 2026, and net cash on the engine's balance-sheet tags. The stock has already re-rated hard on this (roughly doubled off its 2025 lows per Q2 coverage) — the recovery is real but substantially priced.
- Red flags to monitor: federal Medicaid funding policy (the structural shrink in the largest segment), Medicaid rate decisions vs post-redetermination acuity, ACA Marketplace viability if subsidies stay expired, medical-cost trend in behavioral health / home health / high-cost drugs, No Surprises Act dispute costs (management flagged these in Q4 2025 and is litigating), and how much of the 2026 guidance raise is the ~$0.50 of non-recurring items.
- **Hurdle math:** on the engine's numbers the stock clears a 15% IRR at $77.51 (the weighted IV@15%) and trades 11.9% below that figure at $69.29 — but that clearing price inherits the OCF-inflated base, so it overstates the true margin of safety; a margin-of-safety buy price would need to sit materially below the weighted IV@15%, in words, and no hand-computed figure is quoted for it.

## Final verdict
- **Final tier: C** (tier_override from tier-by-numbers B — reason: insurer model mismatch, the same economics as SECTOR_MODEL_MISMATCH though Centene's Healthcare sector does not trip that flag; the OCF-based OE base capitalizes premium/claims working-capital and reserve timing — TTM OE/share $17.55 vs the $8.35 median base and guided FY2026 adjusted EPS above $4.80 shows the spread — and NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE is structural in 2023, 2024 and 2025, so the B overstates distributable owner's earnings; softened one notch, confidence low)
- Confidence: **Low** (insurer OE-model mismatch + scenario spread 4.00x; the direction — recovery underway, roughly fairly priced — is more robust than the level)
- One-liner: Largest US Medicaid MCO, moat 4/10 — engine prints Tier B (weighted IRR 16.42%, IV@15% $77.51 vs $69.29) on an OCF base that capitalizes insurer working-capital/reserve timing, so the final tier is softened to C at low confidence; it clears 15% at ~$77.51 on engine numbers only, with a materially lower true margin of safety.
